desc:
Encoding. A non-negative integer is stored as an array of its decimal digits, most significant digit first, one digit per element, with no leading zeros; the number zero is stored as [0]. Results use the same format. The numbers can have thousands of digits, so you cannot convert a whole array into one machine integer.

Divide the big number a by the big number b and return the quotient rounded down, as a digit array ([0] if a < b). b is never zero. Neither number fits in a machine integer, and you may not use a built-in big-integer type.

Example: a = [1,0,0,0,0], b = [3,0,0]: 10000 / 300 = 33.3..., so the answer is [3,3]. Example: a = [4,2], b = [4,3] gives [0].
constraints: 0 ≤ a[i], b[i] ≤ 9, no leading zeros except for [0]
hints: Long division with a single-digit divisor is easy. A multi-digit divisor needs a way to compare and subtract two digit arrays.
Bring down the digits of a one at a time into a remainder array. Each quotient digit says how many times b fits into the current remainder.

For each new digit: append it to the remainder (drop leading zeros), then while remainder ≥ b subtract b and count. The count is at most 9 because the remainder before appending was smaller than b. Comparison: a longer array is larger, equal lengths compare lexicographically.
editorial: Simulate schoolbook long division. Maintain rem, the remainder of the prefix of a processed so far, always without leading zeros and always smaller than b before the next digit is brought down. After appending the next digit, rem < 10 · b, so at most nine subtractions of b bring it below b again; the number of subtractions is the next quotient digit.

Each subtraction is a column subtraction with a borrow over the last len(b) digits of rem (a borrow may reach one digit further left when rem is one digit longer than b). After subtracting, strip leading zeros of rem so that the length comparison stays valid. Each of the at most n quotient steps does at most nine O(m) subtractions: O(9 · n · m). Finally strip leading zeros of the quotient. A faster approach would estimate each quotient digit from the leading digits (Knuth's algorithm D) but is not needed here.
